summary: Specifies conventions for how S/MIME agents use X.509 certificates, which are central to sending and receiving secure MIME messages. It explains how agents validate certificates according to the Internet PKI profile. It was replaced by RFC 5750.

eli5.summary: Secure email needs ID cards for people. This document says how email programs check those IDs. It was replaced by RFC 5750.

questions: how do email programs check if a certificate is valid
what extensions must s/mime certificates have
subtitle: How S/MIME email agents validate and use X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: S/MIME (Secure MIME) email uses X.509 certificates to sign and encrypt messages. Different S/MIME implementations handle certificates differently, and email agents need clear rules for validating certificates before using the public key to verify signatures or encrypt data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies conventions for how S/MIME agents must validate X.509 certificates according to the Internet PKI profile, handle certificate revocation lists (CRLs), process certificate extensions, and match email addresses in certificates to the message sender.
tldr.outcome: S/MIME email clients now follow consistent rules for certificate validation, improving interoperability. The RFC superseded RFC 2632 and was replaced by RFC 5750.

today: RFC 3850 is a Proposed Standard that specifies S/MIME version 3.1 certificate handling conventions. It was obsoleted by RFC 5750, which provides consolidated and updated S/MIME certificate handling requirements.

sections.title: Certificate Validation in S/MIME
sections.content:
S/MIME agents (email software that sends and receives secure messages) must validate X.509 certificates before using them. Validation means checking that the certificate is signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), that it has not been revoked, and that it is valid at the time of use.

S/MIME agents MUST follow the validation rules in RFC 3280, the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKIX) Certificate and CRL Profile, in addition to the rules in this RFC. The RFC also clarifies changes from S/MIME version 3 (RFC 2632), such as requiring support for version 2 CRLs and attribute certificates, and discouraging the use of MD2 for new signatures.
sections.eli5: Before trusting someone's email ID card, you need to check that it is real, that it has not been taken away, and that it is still good right now.

sections.title: Certificate Processing and Validation
sections.content:
Receiving agents MUST support version 1 and version 3 X.509 certificates. They SHOULD support version 2 attribute certificates. Agents MUST NOT accept PKCS #6 extended certificates or version 1 attribute certificates.

When processing a certificate, the agent must verify the signature on the certificate, check that the certificate chain leads to a trusted CA, and verify the certificate's validity period. For signature verification, agents MUST be capable of verifying signatures made with id-dsa-with-sha1, md5WithRSAEncryption, and sha1WithRSAEncryption with key sizes from 512 to 2048 bits. The use of MD2 for new signatures is discouraged due to known attacks.
sections.eli5: Check that someone signed the ID card with a trustworthy signature, that the signature uses a good math method, and that the ID card has not expired.

sections.title: Certificate Revocation and CRL Processing
sections.content:
Agents MUST support the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) format defined in RFC 3280 and MUST perform revocation status checking in accordance with that RFC. Both version 1 and version 2 CRLs MUST be supported. Agents SHOULD retrieve CRL information every time a certificate is verified, even if the certificate was verified previously.

If a certificate cannot be verified or has been revoked, the agent MUST inform the user in a clear way. Because older CRLs may not include recent revocations, agents SHOULD check for the most recently issued CRL for a CA. Receiving agents SHOULD cache CRLs received in messages for use in processing later messages.
sections.eli5: Keep a list of ID cards that were cancelled. Check this list every time you verify someone's card, because new cards get cancelled regularly.

sections.title: Email Address Matching and Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
The email address SHOULD be placed in the subjectAltName extension and SHOULD NOT be in the certificate's distinguished name. Agents MUST recognize and accept certificates that contain no email address. When an email address is present, receiving agents MUST check that the address in the email's From or Sender header matches an Internet mail address in the signer's certificate.

The RFC requires correct handling of certificate extensions: basicConstraints, keyUsage, authorityKeyIdentifier, subjectKeyIdentifier, and subjectAltName. If a key usage extension is present, it MUST be marked critical and agents MUST NOT accept a signature using a certificate without the digitalSignature or nonRepudiation bit set. For the extendedKeyUsage extension, S/MIME agents MUST check for either emailProtection or anyExtendedKeyUsage OID.
sections.eli5: Make sure the email address on the ID card matches who says they sent the email. Also check special markings on the ID card that say what it can be used for.

sections.title: Certificate Storage and Retrieval
sections.content:
Agents SHOULD provide a mechanism to store and retrieve certificates for correspondents, such as a local certificate database similar to an address book. When receiving a signed message, agents SHOULD cache the certificates in the message for use in validating later messages and optionally store them for future use.

Sending agents SHOULD include the sender's certificate and issuer certificates in signed messages to help recipients establish trust in the sender's public key. This is especially important when sending to new recipients or when the recipient may not have access to the certificate through other means. A sending agent SHOULD include at least one chain of certificates up to, but not including, a CA that the sender believes the recipient trusts.
sections.eli5: Save copies of ID cards from emails you receive so you can check future emails from the same people. When you send secure email, include a copy of your own ID card so the receiver can check it.
